PARTITION BY defines the group, ORDER BY defines the frame; windows run after GROUP BY/HAVING, before ORDER BY ( Postgres tutorial ). Running total: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY dt ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) — every row survives, unlike GROUP BY. RANK vs DENSE_RANK on scores 100,100,90 : RANK → 1,1,3 ; DENSE_RANK → 1,1,2 . Function Returns Typical use ROW_NUMBER() 1,2,3 — unique per partition dedup, latest record per key RANK() / DENSE_RANK() ties share rank; gaps vs no gaps: 1,1,3 vs 1,1,2 rankings, tiers, percentiles LAG(col) / LEAD(col) previous / next row value deltas, session starts The Classic Problems ​ Worked Example Dedup — latest order per customer. Naive self-join: the correlated subquery re-scans the table per row, and ties return duplicates. SELECT o.* FROM orders o WHERE o.order_ts = (SELECT MAX(order_ts) FROM orders i WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id); Windowed: one scan plus one sort, deterministic tie-break, exactly one row per key even on ties. SELECT * FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC, id DESC) AS rn FROM orders) t WHERE rn = 1; The window wins because it does a single pass instead of a correlated re-scan per row, makes ties deterministic, and never duplicates rows. Snowflake and Databricks SQL collapse it further with QUALIFY (OSS Spark has no QUALIFY): SELECT * FROM orders QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC, id DESC) = 1; Use cases: Dedup: latest record per key from append-only sources. Sessionization: gap-based sessions from clickstream timestamps. Cumulative KPIs: running totals, month-over-month deltas via LAG. Top-N dashboards: top 3 products per region ( ROW_NUMBER ... WHERE rn <= N ). -- increment a counter at every >30min gap; running sum = session id SELECT user_id, ts, SUM(CASE WHEN ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) > INTERVAL 30 MINUTE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS session_id FROM clicks; GROUP BY traps: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after — aggregates are illegal in WHERE. COUNT(col) skips NULLs, COUNT(*) counts rows, NULL is its own group; every SELECT column must be grouped or aggregated (Spark enforces strictly; Snowflake offers ANY_VALUE ). Join anti-patterns: LEFT JOIN plus WHERE on the right table's column silently becomes an INNER JOIN — move the condition into ON. Duplicate join keys cause row fan-out (a 1.1x key duplication silently doubles revenue sums); non-equi and comma joins degrade to nested loops or cross joins. PARTITION BY defines the group, ORDER BY defines the frame; windows run after GROUP BY/HAVING, before ORDER BY ( Postgres tutorial ). Running total: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY dt ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) — every row survives, unlike GROUP BY. RANK vs DENSE_RANK on scores 100,100,90 : RANK → 1,1,3 ; DENSE_RANK → 1,1,2 . Function Returns Typical use ROW_NUMBER() 1,2,3 — unique per partition dedup, latest record per key RANK() / DENSE_RANK() ties share rank; gaps vs no gaps: 1,1,3 vs 1,1,2 rankings, tiers, percentiles LAG(col) / LEAD(col) previous / next row value deltas, session starts The Classic Problems ​ Worked Example Dedup — latest order per customer. Naive self-join: the correlated subquery re-scans the table per row, and ties return duplicates. SELECT o.* FROM orders o WHERE o.order_ts = (SELECT MAX(order_ts) FROM orders i WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id); Windowed: one scan plus one sort, deterministic tie-break, exactly one row per key even on ties. SELECT * FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC, id DESC) AS rn FROM orders) t WHERE rn = 1; The window wins because it does a single pass instead of a correlated re-scan per row, makes ties deterministic, and never duplicates rows. Sessionization: gap-based sessions from clickstream timestamps. Cumulative KPIs: running totals, month-over-month deltas via LAG. Top-N dashboards: top 3 products per region ( ROW_NUMBER ... WHERE rn <= N ). -- increment a counter at every >30min gap; running sum = session id SELECT user_id, ts, SUM(CASE WHEN ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) > INTERVAL 30 MINUTE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS session_id FROM clicks; GROUP BY traps: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after — aggregates are illegal in WHERE. COUNT(col) skips NULLs, COUNT(*) counts rows, NULL is its own group; every SELECT column must be grouped or aggregated (Spark enforces strictly; Snowflake offers ANY_VALUE ). Join anti-patterns: LEFT JOIN plus WHERE on the right table's column silently becomes an INNER JOIN — move the condition into ON. Duplicate join keys cause row fan-out (a 1.1x key duplication silently doubles revenue sums); non-equi and comma joins degrade to nested loops or cross joins. availability) or AP (serve possibly stale data, sacrifice consistency). "CA" is only coherent for non-distributed systems with no partitions ( CAP theorem ). "C" here means linearizability ( Gilbert–Lynch proof ); the practical spectrum from Jepsen is: strong → sequential → causal → eventual. Read-your-writes is the pragmatic middle users actually need: a session sees its own writes without global coordination. ACID vs BASE ( Vogels, Eventually-Consistent ): Model Core promise Cost ACID Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable per transaction Locks + coordination + latency BASE Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent Stale reads, app-level conflict handling Consistency level Guarantee Tools that offer it Linearizable Every read sees latest committed write ZooKeeper, etcd, Spanner Sequential Per-partition/client order kept, no cross-client causality Kafka per-partition ordering Causal / read-your-writes See effects of causes you observed DynamoDB strongly consistent reads, MongoDB causal sessions Eventual Replicas converge when writes stop Cassandra ONE (tunable), Redis replicas, DynamoDB default reads flowchart TD REQ[Request arrives at cluster] --> P{Network partition now} P -- No partition --> OK[CA is possible - serve consistent and available] P -- Partition --> CH{Pick one} CH -- Consistency --> CP[CP - block or reject rather than serve stale] CH -- Availability --> AP[AP - answer with possibly stale data] CP --> EX1[Examples - ZooKeeper - etcd - HBase - Kafka min ISR] AP --> EX2[Examples - Cassandra - DynamoDB - DNS] Replication & Partitioning ​ Leader–follower replication: sync (follower acks before commit — no loss, higher latency) vs async (fast, but failover loses recent writes and lagging followers serve stale reads). Semi-sync is the middle ground. Quorum rule: R + W > N forces read and write sets to overlap; W > N/2 prevents two write quorums (split-brain). "fail", "choice": true, "loop": false}], "start": "start"} Batch: Scheduled, Bounded, Reproducible ​ Input bounded, job runs to termination. Triggered on a cadence (Airflow/dbt/cron) with a logical execution date : the 3am Feb 5 run processes Feb 4's partition. Windows = partition filters : WHERE dt = '2026-05-01' . No late-data problem — the window "closes" only when the job runs, long after all data landed. Backfill is the killer feature : fix logic, rerun old partitions, overwrite outputs. Deterministic code over bounded input → reproducible results. Retry safety = idempotency. Non-idempotent INSERT INTO + retry silently double-counts — the classic batch production bug. -- rerun-safe patterns; key outputs by (pipeline, logical partition) INSERT OVERWRITE daily_metrics SELECT ... WHERE dt = '2026-05-01'; -- replace MERGE INTO daily_metrics t USING staged s ON t.dt = s.dt WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE ...; -- keyed merge Latency: minutes–hours (schedule + runtime). Cost per TB: lowest — spot instances, columnar scans, no per-record overhead. Streaming: Event Time, Watermarks, State ​ Time domain Definition Use for Event time When the event occurred (device clock) Correctness: windows, billing, analytics Processing time When the system sees the event Lag monitoring, alerting Ingestion time When the pipeline received it Compromise; rarely correct Events arrive out of order (offline mobile, retries, cross-region): a 10:00:00 click processed at 10:00:41. Only event time is reproducible. Watermark W = maxObservedEventTime − allowedLateness (typically 20 s–5 min): monotonic promise "no event ≤ W arrives later"; window emits when W passes its end ( Flink event time ). Too tight → drops; too loose → delayed results + longer state. Parallel pipelines: W = min across partitions — one idle source stalls progress. State (window contents, join buffers, dedup keys) lives keyed in RocksDB/heap; needs TTL or it grows forever. Checkpoints (Flink aligned barriers): async distributed snapshot of state + source offsets; on failure restore and replay from Kafka ( checkpoint docs ). processing time ----------------------------> events: e1@10:00:03 e2@10:01:10 e3@10:04:50 e4@10:04:58(LATE) watermark W: 10:02:30 10:03:40 10:07:00

can't hold logs, JSON, images, ML assets Lake 2010s: HDFS → S3 + Spark Cheap open storage, land anything, schema-on-read Transactions, quality, governance → swamps Cloud DW 2015: Snowflake, BigQuery Storage/compute split, elasticity, near-zero ops Proprietary formats; lake + warehouse = two copies Lakehouse 2020: Iceberg, Delta, Hudi ACID + time travel on open Parquet ( CIDR 2021 , Iceberg docs ) Still maturing: compaction, catalogs, write concurrency Lakehouse = open file format (Parquet) + transactional table format + object storage + catalog + any engine (Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, and the warehouses themselves). The table format becomes the platform; warehouses become engines over it. Why Data Lakes Failed ​ 60–85% of big-data-era projects were abandoned; the swamp was structural, not operator error ( arXiv retrospective ): No atomic commits — concurrent writers corrupted partitions; readers saw partial files (worse pre-Dec-2020 S3 eventual consistency). No schema enforcement — schema-on-read means the writer checks nothing; a renamed column silently poisons every downstream job. No performance layer — no stats, no pruning, no compaction → millions of small files, full-partition scans. No governance — duplicate contradictory datasets; the "single source of truth" silently stayed in the EDW → paying for two synced copies. Hive Metastore was a partition directory, not a transactional catalog — no commit protocol, MySQL-backed SPOF. Successor: REST catalogs ( Iceberg REST, Unity, Polaris). Interview trap Blaming "bad engineers" for lake failure is the junior answer. The platform made hygiene expensive and sloppiness free — at scale, the equilibrium is a swamp. Name the structural mechanisms. Architecture: Coupled vs Disaggregated ​ Shared-nothing MPP (Teradata, classic Redshift): node owns disk + CPU. Fastest per-dollar at steady state; adding nodes forces rebalancing; storage growth forces compute growth. Disaggregated (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks ): stateless clusters query immutable files on object storage through a cache. Compute and storage scale independently, per-second. Architecture: Two Different Answers ​ SNOWFLAKE DATABRICKS ┌───────────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────────┐ │ Cloud services: optimizer │ │ Control plane: UC, SQL │ │ Virtual warehouses XS-6XL │ │ Spark + Photon clusters │ │ Storage: micro-partitions │ │ Your S3 + Delta ACID log │ │ Bundled bill │ │ Unbundled: DBU + VM bill │ └───────────────────────────┘ └───────────────────────────┘ Snowflake : storage/compute/cloud-services decoupled; warehouses (XS→6XL) auto-suspend to zero; micro-partitions (~16 MB, min/max pruning) remove partition design; Time Travel + zero-copy cloning included. Databricks : control plane + Spark/Photon compute over your S3/ADLS/GCS; Delta Lake transaction log gives ACID with optimistic concurrency; Photon (C++ vectorized) is why its SQL got competitive. Deepest difference: Snowflake abstracts storage away; Databricks makes your lake the source of truth — that choice explains pricing, governance, and lock-in below. Sharing data between them is the 2025–26 pain: Snowflake native tables are proprietary and Spark can't scan them efficiently; the neutral pattern is Iceberg + REST catalog (Open Catalog/Polaris or UC) with both engines reading. No atomicity/isolation — multi-file commits crash into half-states; S3/GCS/Azure have no atomic directory rename, and readers listing mid-write see torn state. No updates/deletes — files are immutable; row-level changes mean whole-file rewrites with no invalidation protocol. No schema/partition evolution — repartitioning = full rewrite or broken readers. Planning is O(all files) — engines list directories and read footers; millions of files dominate query latency. Delta Lake: One Transaction Log ​ Whole architecture = _delta_log/ : each commit appends 000...N.json with atomic actions — add (data file + stats), remove , metaData , txn (idempotent streaming), commitInfo . Checkpoint every 10th commit ( 000...10.parquet ) — readers replay ≤10 JSONs instead of thousands; current state = deterministic replay of the log. Writers use optimistic concurrency : attempt commit by creating file N+1; conditional put / catalog conflict manager arbitrates; losers re-validate against new state and retry. Deletes : copy-on-write historically; since Delta 2.x, Deletion Vectors (Roaring bitmaps as side files, referenced from add actions) make DELETE / MERGE metadata + bitmap only ( delta.io ). Liquid clustering (GA DBR 15.4+) supersedes ZORDER ; time travel via VERSION AS OF , retention via VACUUM + logRetentionDuration . Ecosystem : Linux-Foundation-governed ( 2019 announcement ); delta-rs powers Python deltalake , Polars, DuckDB's Delta extension ( DuckDB docs ); UniForm exposes a Delta table as Iceberg — same Parquet, generated metadata ( Databricks docs ). DataFrame]] --> U[Unresolved Logical Plan] AN --> |analyzer resolves catalog| AN[Analyzed Logical Plan] AN --> |rule batches to fixed point| OPT[Optimized Logical Plan] OPT --> |cost based JoinSelection| PH[Physical Plan] PH --> AQE[AdaptiveSparkPlan] AQE --> |whole-stage codegen| EX[Executed stages] EX -. completed shuffle stats .-> AQE ‹ › Rule-based optimizer: batches of Rule[LogicalPlan] applied to a fixed point — no statistics needed ( SQL docs ): Rule What it does Example PredicatePushdown filters before join/exchange WHERE on partition column prunes files ColumnPruning reads only referenced columns parquet scan of 3 of 200 columns ConstantFolding folds literal math / dead branches WHERE 1 = 0 → empty relation Cost-based physical planning: JoinSelection compares plan sizes from catalog stats ( sizeInBytes , rowCount ); spark.sql.cbo.enabled (default false ) enables richer stats. Without ANALYZE TABLE , sizeInBytes defaults to a huge value → auto-broadcast never fires at compile time. Whole-stage codegen fuses all operators of one stage into a single Java function — no per-row virtual dispatch; falls back above spark.sql.codegen.maxFields (100). Read it in explain("formatted") : look for PushedFilters , the ReadSchema column list, the number of Exchange nodes, and the * codegen marker — abridged: == Physical Plan == <- isFinalPlan=true means AQE re-planned AdaptiveSparkPlan (6) +- Sort (5) +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 4096) <- each Exchange = a stage cut +- Project (3) <- ColumnPruning happened +- Filter (2) <- Pushdown happened +- Scan parquet (1) PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(customer_id)] ReadSchema: struct<customer_id:string,amount:decimal(10,2)> Tungsten carries this to hardware: sun.misc.Unsafe off-heap allocation, a compact binary row format ( UnsafeRow ) instead of JVM objects, and cache-aware computation ( Databricks, Project Tungsten ) — GC pressure drops because data stops living as objects. AQE: Adaptive Query Execution ​ Re-optimizes at each shuffle boundary using actual map-output stats from completed stages ( performance tuning docs , Databricks AQE ); on by default since 3.2.0 ( spark.sql.adaptive.enabled ). true, "loop": false}], "start": "produce"} Queues, Pub/Sub, and Logs ​ Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ): each message to exactly one consumer, ack-then-delete, no replay. Pub/sub : every subscriber gets every event; broker tracks subscriptions, not replay positions. Log (Kafka): append-only, ordered per partition; consumer-owned offsets make replay an offset reset, not a redeliver. Push vs pull : push (RabbitMQ) = lower latency, credit/prefetch flow control; pull (Kafka, SQS long-poll ≤20s) = consumer-paced batching and trivial replay. Ordering : strict only within a partition ; hash(key) % partitionCount gives per-entity order — and changing partition count silently breaks that key→partition map. Kafka Internals: Partitions, ISR, Offsets ​ Topic → partitions → segments : each partition is an append-only log split into ~1 GB segment files ( log.segment.bytes ) plus sparse offset and time indexes. Deletes/compaction work at segment granularity, never in-place — the whole reason writes are sequential I/O. Page cache + zero-copy : Kafka caches nothing itself; hot tail reads hit the OS page cache (small JVM heap, no GC pressure) and sendfile() ships bytes disk→socket without user-space copies (disabled under TLS). Replication : one leader per partition; followers fetch continuously. Replicas current within replica.lag.time.max.ms (30s) form the ISR . The high watermark is the highest offset replicated to all ISR — consumers read only up to HW. Leader dies → controller elects from ISR; unclean.leader.election.enable=false (default) trades availability for zero acknowledged-data loss. Offsets : consumers commit to __consumer_offsets , a 50-partition log-compacted internal topic. Retention & compaction : retention.ms / retention.bytes per partition (default 7 days). Compaction keeps only the latest value per key plus tombstones for deletes; requires keyed records; used for __consumer_offsets , state-store changelogs, entity/CDC topics. Tiered storage (KIP-405, GA 3.6+): local disk keeps recent segments, older offloaded to S3/GCS — retention decoupled from broker disk. KRaft (KIP-500): a Raft metadata quorum replaces ZooKeeper — production-ready in 3.3, ZooKeeper removed entirely in Kafka 4.0 (2025) ( upgrade guide , [KIP-500](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-500%3A+Replace+ZooKeeper+with+a+Self-Managed+Metadata+ Quorum )). Pub/sub : every subscriber gets every event; broker tracks subscriptions, not replay positions. Log (Kafka): append-only, ordered per partition; consumer-owned offsets make replay an offset reset, not a redeliver. Push vs pull : push (RabbitMQ) = lower latency, credit/prefetch flow control; pull (Kafka, SQS long-poll ≤20s) = consumer-paced batching and trivial replay. Ordering : strict only within a partition ; hash(key) % partitionCount gives per-entity order — and changing partition count silently breaks that key→partition map. Kafka Internals: Partitions, ISR, Offsets ​ Topic → partitions → segments : each partition is an append-only log split into ~1 GB segment files ( log.segment.bytes ) plus sparse offset and time indexes. Deletes/compaction work at segment granularity, never in-place — the whole reason writes are sequential I/O. Page cache + zero-copy : Kafka caches nothing itself; hot tail reads hit the OS page cache (small JVM heap, no GC pressure) and sendfile() ships bytes disk→socket without user-space copies (disabled under TLS). Replication : one leader per partition; followers fetch continuously. Replicas current within replica.lag.time.max.ms (30s) form the ISR . The high watermark is the highest offset replicated to all ISR — consumers read only up to HW. Leader dies → controller elects from ISR; unclean.leader.election.enable=false (default) trades availability for zero acknowledged-data loss. Offsets : consumers commit to __consumer_offsets , a 50-partition log-compacted internal topic. Retention & compaction : retention.ms / retention.bytes per partition (default 7 days). tests, and Soda all map to them): Dimension Question it answers Real failure example Typical check Accuracy Does data match reality? FX rate stored as 1.10 vs true 1.01 Sample-diff against trusted source Completeness Are all expected rows present? 2.1M rows land vs 2.4M in source Row-count ratio, NOT NULL Freshness How recent is the data? Dashboard serves yesterday's noon snapshot max(event_ts) vs now Validity Are values well-formed and in range? Negative ages, emails without @ Schema, regex, range tests Uniqueness Any duplicates from retries? Kafka at-least-once → double-loaded partition Primary-key uniqueness test Consistency Do systems agree with each other? Warehouse revenue ≠ app-DB revenue Cross-system reconciliation Use cases: GDPR-delete audit trail → lineage + a uniqueness check on user_id proves the delete propagated to every derived table. Finance-grade reconciliation → accuracy + consistency: checksums and source-vs-target diffs, not just row counts. ML feature freshness → freshness SLIs on feature tables; stale features silently degrade model quality. Testing Pyramid for Data ​ Fast and cheap at the base, expensive and rare at the top — run the base on every commit, the top in production: Layer Scope Example When it runs Unit tests Transform logic in isolation Spark UDF / dbt macro against fixture input, edge cases (nulls, dupes, tz) Every PR (CI) Data tests Assertions on real data unique , not_null , accepted_values , relationships Every pipeline run Integration / reconciliation End-to-end truth Source-vs-target row counts + checksums on a small fixture Daily / before publish Production monitoring Live anomalies Freshness lag, volume spikes, quarantine rate Continuous -- dbt tests: YAML-declared SQL assertions that gate a model's publish models: - name: fct_orders columns: - order_id: tests: [unique, not_null] - status: tests: - accepted_values: [placed, shipped, refunded] Great Expectations : Python expectations-as-code with rich data docs; best inside ingestion/ Spark /Airflow jobs. dbt tests : SQL-native, live next to the models they gate; best for warehouse layers. Soda : YAML SodaCL checks including freshness and anomaly scans; lightweight, pipeline-friendly ( Soda docs ). Observability: Metrics, Lineage, Alerts ​ Three pillars — metrics tell you what broke, logs where , lineage what else is impacted: Metrics : rows in/out, bytes, run duration, freshness lag, quarantine rate, test pass rate. FX rate stored as 1.10 vs true 1.01 Sample-diff against trusted source Completeness Are all expected rows present? 2.1M rows land vs 2.4M in source Row-count ratio, NOT NULL Freshness How recent is the data? Dashboard serves yesterday's noon snapshot max(event_ts) vs now Validity Are values well-formed and in range? Negative ages, emails without @ Schema, regex, range tests Uniqueness Any duplicates from retries? Kafka at-least-once → double-loaded partition Primary-key uniqueness test Consistency Do systems agree with each other? Warehouse revenue ≠ app-DB revenue Cross-system reconciliation Use cases: GDPR-delete audit trail → lineage + a uniqueness check on user_id proves the delete propagated to every derived table. Finance-grade reconciliation → accuracy + consistency: checksums and source-vs-target diffs, not just row counts. ML feature freshness → freshness SLIs on feature tables; stale features silently degrade model quality. Soda : YAML SodaCL checks including freshness and anomaly scans; lightweight, pipeline-friendly ( Soda docs ). "metrics fail" .-> D Seven steps every chapter follows: clarifying requirements, framing as ML task, data preparation, model development, evaluation, deployment/serving, monitoring/infrastructure (ch1, p2). Clarifying-question menu: business objective, features to support, data sources/labels, constraints (compute, on-device), scale, performance (accuracy vs latency) (ch1 §Clarifying Requirements, p1-2). The load-bearing move is translating business goal → trainable ML objective (Table 1.1, p3): "increase engagement" → "maximize watch time"; "protect privacy" → "detect faces/plates accurately". Data engineering vocabulary expected: ETL , structured vs unstructured data (ch1, p7-9). Requirements & Problem Framing ​ Scope from clarifying questions: 4 languages (EN/ES/KO/FR), auto language detection (users can't always name the language), inputs up to 1,000 words, cloud-deployed (no on-device), no real-time initially (ch3 §Clarifying Requirements). Training data: 300M sentence pairs + terabytes of general per-language text (ch3 §Clarifying Requirements). Task shape: sequence-to-sequence — input and output sequences of different lengths ; encoder-decoder splits the job: encoder builds context vectors from the source, decoder emits target tokens one at a time (ch3 §Frame the Problem as an ML Task). Why encoder-decoder over encoder-only/decoder-only: (1) separation of input understanding (bidirectional) from output generation, (2) natural variable-length I/O, (3) cross-attention lets the decoder focus on relevant source parts while generating (ch3 §Choosing a suitable ML approach). Transformers beat GRU/LSTM on long-range dependencies; attention itself was introduced for translation ( arXiv 1409.0473 ). Data Preparation ​ Keep: remove missing/noisy pairs (HTML tags, wrong language pairing), dedup, replace named entities with ENTITY_1 -style placeholders, restored after translation (ch3 §Text preprocessing). Drop (legacy steps): lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming/lemmatization, punctuation removal — all lose grammatical/case information modern Transformers learn from context (ch3 §Text preprocessing). Tokenization Vocabulary OOV handling Word-level Hundreds of thousands across languages — huge, inefficient Fails on unseen words Subword (BPE) Compact, built by iterative merges Rare/unseen words decompose into known pieces ( BPE, HF course ) (ch3 §Text tokenization) BPE mechanics: start from characters + </w> boundary token; repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until vocab target size. </w> distinguishes "cat" as a full word from "cat" as a prefix of another word (ch3 §Byte-Pair Encoding). Resulting training data: one table per language pair; each row = two token-ID sequences (source, target) (ch3 §Data Preparation, Fig. 11). Model Development ​ Encoder (per block): embed -> +positional (fixed sine-cosine) -> MHA self-attention -> FFN [x N] Decoder (per block): masked self-attention -> CROSS-attention over encoder output -> FFN -> linear+softmax head Key differences: cross-attention layer | unidirectional (masked) self-attention | prediction head (ch3 §Architecture) Encoder: bidirectional self-attention — every token sees all tokens; 1,000-word cap means standard attention suffices, no optimized attention needed (ch3 §Encoder). Decoder: masks future tokens (generation must only use already-generated prefixes) (ch3 §Decoder). Two-stage training (ch3 §Training): Stage Data Objective Loss 1. Unsupervised pretraining C4, Wikipedia, StackExchange — keep only target languages, drop the rest Masked LM — mask input tokens, decoder predicts them (next-token would let the encoder "cheat" by leaking the answer) Cross-entropy on masked positions only 2. Supervised finetuning 300M translation pairs, per language pair Next-token prediction on target sentence Cross-entropy over all positions Skip pretraining cost: start from public encoder-decoder checkpoints (T5, BART ) (ch3 §Training). Bilingual vs multilingual finetuning (ch3 §Training): Bilingual (one model per pair) Multilingual (one model, many pairs) Accuracy Higher — captures pair-specific nuances Often matches (mT5, mBART ) and improving Ops cost N-pair models to train/deploy/maintain One model — cheaper, simpler Debuggability Issues isolated per pair Cross-pair interference Pick ✔ accuracy prioritized — flowchart LR IN[Input sentence] --> DET[Language detector - encoder-only classifier] DET -- detected language --> ROUTE{Translation service\nroutes by detected + desired pair} ROUTE --> M[Per-pair encoder-decoder model] M --> BS[Beam search decoding] BS --> TK[Detokenize IDs to text] TK --> OUT[Translation to user] 🧭 Scenario · Serve a four-language translation service − 100% + ✎ ↺ ◉ {"title": "Serve a four-language translation service", "nodes": [{"id": "detect", "label": "Auto-detect the source language", "cap": "Users can't always name the language — an encoder-only classifier routes by detected + desired pair"}, {"id": "fleet", "label": "One model or one per pair?", "cap": "Bilingual: higher accuracy, N models to train and maintain; Section 18 of 26 Machine Translation (Google Translate) A seq2seq translation service is the canonical encoder-decoder design — interviewers use it to test architecture selection, two-stage training, and evaluation metrics; the same skeleton covers summarization and speech recognition. Requirements & Problem Framing ​ Scope from clarifying questions: 4 languages (EN/ES/KO/FR), auto language detection (users can't always name the language), inputs up to 1,000 words, cloud-deployed (no on-device), no real-time initially (ch3 §Clarifying Requirements). Training data: 300M sentence pairs + terabytes of general per-language text (ch3 §Clarifying Requirements). Task shape: sequence-to-sequence — input and output sequences of different lengths ; encoder-decoder splits the job: encoder builds context vectors from the source, decoder emits target tokens one at a time (ch3 §Frame the Problem as an ML Task). Why encoder-decoder over encoder-only/decoder-only: (1) separation of input understanding (bidirectional) from output generation, (2) natural variable-length I/O, (3) cross-attention lets the decoder focus on relevant source parts while generating (ch3 §Choosing a suitable ML approach). Transformers beat GRU/LSTM on long-range dependencies; attention itself was introduced for translation ( arXiv 1409.0473 ). Data Preparation ​ Keep: remove missing/noisy pairs (HTML tags, wrong language pairing), dedup, replace named entities with ENTITY_1 -style placeholders, restored after translation (ch3 §Text preprocessing). Drop (legacy steps): lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming/lemmatization, punctuation removal — all lose grammatical/case information modern Transformers learn from context (ch3 §Text preprocessing). Tokenization Vocabulary OOV handling Word-level Hundreds of thousands across languages — huge, inefficient Fails on unseen words Subword (BPE) Compact, built by iterative merges Rare/unseen words decompose into known pieces ( BPE, HF course ) (ch3 §Text tokenization) BPE mechanics: start from characters + </w> boundary token; repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until vocab target size. </w> distinguishes "cat" as a full word from "cat" as a prefix of another word (ch3 §Byte-Pair Encoding). Resulting training data: one table per language pair; each row = two token-ID sequences (source, target) (ch3 §Data Preparation, Fig. 11). x: Section 20 of 26 Image Captioning A multi-modal encoder–decoder design: the image is treated as a foreign "language" that one encoder speaks and one decoder translates. The reusable muscles — cleaning 400M noisy pairs, picking encoder output granularity, consensus-based evaluation, and confidence-gated serving — mirror the data-quality and evaluation discipline a DE design round probes. Requirements Snapshot ​ Clarify before designing; each answer removes a design branch (ch5 §Clarifying Requirements): Question Answer Design consequence Image domain General everyday images No domain-specific finetuning Use case Asset name suggestions for uploaded files Short, descriptive captions — summarize long ones Language English only Filter non-English pairs Data 400M pairs, unpreprocessed: mixed languages, noisy/inaccurate, some missing Heavy cleaning pipeline (below) Latency 1–2 s acceptable, not real-time Beam search affordable at serving Ambiguous images Skip the suggestion Confidence threshold gates the output Fairness/safety No biased or offensive captions Post-processing filter required Min resolution 256×256 Drop smaller images in prep Applications beyond user-facing: NSFW moderation via text-based interpretation, and fixing the cold-start problem in recommenders — captions give textual features for new items (ch5 §Introduction). Data Preparation (400M Noisy Pairs) ​ Caption preparation (ch5 §Caption preparation): Remove non-English captions — model scope is English. Deduplicate : duplicate images via perceptual hashing or a CLIP image encoder; duplicate captions via exact match or CLIP text-encoder semantic similarity. Duplicates cause overfitting to redundant pairs. Remove irrelevant pairs : pretrained vision–language model (CLIP) scores image–caption relevance; drop pairs below a threshold (e.g., 0.25 ). CLIP scoring details: ch9. Summarize long captions with an LLM (e.g., Llama) — training on long captions teaches the model to emit long captions, wrong for the use case. Normalize (lowercase, trim whitespace), then tokenize with subword BPE (details: ch2–3). Image preparation (ch5 §Image preparation): drop <256×256; normalize pixels to 0–1; drop blurry/over-/underexposed images scored by quality models like the LAION Aesthetics Predictor ; then make dimensions uniform without breaking aspect ratio: Resize + center-crop (target 256x256), original 512x768: 1. resize so the SMALLER side matches target: 512x768 -> 256x384 2. center-crop the long side: 256x384 -> 256x256 Architecture: Encoder–Decoder, Two Modalities ​ Like translation, but the source "language" is pixels (ch5 §Frame the Problem as an ML Task): an image encoder compresses the image, a text decoder generates the caption from those embeddings. Encoder output granularity is the pivotal trade-off (ch5 §Image encoder): Dimension Single token (one vector) Sequence of tokens (per patch) Representation Global summary of whole image Global + local features per region Cost Simple, low compute/resources Higher compute Caption quality Concise, high-level, but generic; loses local detail Descriptive, attends per region Fit to decoder Weak — attention wants sequences Aligns with Transformer attention Encoder backbone choice (ch5 §Image encoder): Dimension CNN-based Transformer-based (ViT) Mechanism Convolutional filters; spatial hierarchies Self-attention over patch embeddings Coverage Local patterns strong; struggles with long-range dependencies Local + global relationships Output shape Grid of feature vectors, e.g. 3×3×c → flatten to 9×c Sequence of c-dim embeddings Patchify converts an image to a sequence in three steps: divide into fixed-size patches → flatten → linearly project. Example: 256×256 image, 64×64 patches → 16 patches, each flattened to 4096-dim then projected to c (ch5 §Patchify, Fig. 9). Positional encoding options: 1D (sequence position; may miss 2D spatial structure) vs 2D (row+col → vector; preserves spatial layout); learnable vs fixed (e.g., sine–cosine). ViT uses learnable 1D; there is no universal best — test combinations (ch5 §Positional encoding). Text decoder : decoder-only Transformer — the standard text-generation choice — consuming the image-embedding sequence and emitting the caption one token at a time (ch5 §Text decoder). Training & Sampling ​ Two-stage strategy, the same pattern as earlier designs (ch5 §Training): Unsupervised pretraining — decoder-only Transformer on general text for language structure. Too expensive to redo: start from pretrained GPT-2 or Llama ; likewise initialize the encoder from pretrained CLIP or ViT . Supervised finetuning — train encoder + decoder jointly on the 400M pairs; encoder learns to encode images, decoder to read image embeddings and emit captions. Objective: next-token prediction with cross-entropy loss (ch5 §ML objective and loss function). Sampling: use beam search , not stochastic sampling (ch5 §Sampling): Reason Why it matters here Quality Higher-quality captions for accurate image description Consistency Deterministic — same image always yields the same caption Coherence Avoids contradictions like "A person is walking house" Evaluation ​ Validation data: held-out images with multiple reference captions from several annotators — multiple references make training robust to phrasing variety and evaluation fairer (ch5 §Offline evaluation metrics, Fig. 14). Metrics: BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR (ch3) plus CIDEr , built specifically for captioning (ch5 §CIDEr). CIDEr steps: 1. TF-IDF: caption + each reference -> numerical vectors 2. Cosine similarity: generated vs each reference (1 = close, 0 = far) 3. Aggregate: average similarities; final CIDEr = mean over validation set Worked example: scores 0.688, 0.257, 0.766 vs 3 refs CIDEr = (0.688 + 0.257 + 0.766) / 3 = 0.570 CIDEr pros CIDEr cons Consensus-based — rewards captions matching multiple references Computationally complex at scale (TF-IDF over large sets) TF-IDF weights rare/important words appropriately Sensitive to reference

Deduplicate : duplicate images via perceptual hashing or a CLIP image encoder; duplicate captions via exact match or CLIP text-encoder semantic similarity. CLIP scoring details: ch9. Summarize long captions with an LLM (e.g., Llama) — training on long captions teaches the model to emit long captions, wrong for the use case. Encoder output granularity is the pivotal trade-off (ch5 §Image encoder): Dimension Single token (one vector) Sequence of tokens (per patch) Representation Global summary of whole image Global + local features per region Cost Simple, low compute/resources Higher compute Caption quality Concise, high-level, but generic; loses local detail Descriptive, attends per region Fit to decoder Weak — attention wants sequences Aligns with Transformer attention Encoder backbone choice (ch5 §Image encoder): Dimension CNN-based Transformer-based (ViT) Mechanism Convolutional filters; spatial hierarchies Self-attention over patch embeddings Coverage Local patterns strong; struggles with long-range dependencies Local + global relationships Output shape Grid of feature vectors, e.g. 3×3×c → flatten to 9×c Sequence of c-dim embeddings Patchify converts an image to a sequence in three steps: divide into fixed-size patches → flatten → linearly project. Example: 256×256 image, 64×64 patches → 16 patches, each flattened to 4096-dim then projected to c (ch5 §Patchify, Fig. 9). Text decoder : decoder-only Transformer — the standard text-generation choice — consuming the image-embedding sequence and emitting the caption one token at a time (ch5 §Text decoder). Too expensive to redo: start from pretrained GPT-2 or Llama ; likewise initialize the encoder from pretrained CLIP or ViT . Supervised finetuning — train encoder + decoder jointly on the 400M pairs; encoder learns to encode images, decoder to read image embeddings and emit captions. Objective: next-token prediction with cross-entropy loss (ch5 §ML objective and loss function). Sampling: use beam search , not stochastic sampling (ch5 §Sampling): Reason Why it matters here Quality Higher-quality captions for accurate image description Consistency Deterministic — same image always yields the same caption Coherence Avoids contradictions like "A person is walking house" Evaluation ​ Validation data: held-out images with multiple reference captions from several annotators — multiple references make training robust to phrasing variety and evaluation fairer (ch5 §Offline evaluation metrics, Fig. 14). Metrics: BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR (ch3) plus CIDEr , built specifically for captioning (ch5 §CIDEr). CIDEr steps: 1. TF-IDF: caption + each reference -> numerical vectors 2. Cosine similarity: generated vs each reference (1 = close, 0 = far) 3. Aggregate: average similarities; final CIDEr = mean over validation set Worked example: scores 0.688, 0.257, 0.766 vs 3 refs CIDEr = (0.688 + 0.257 + 0.766) / 3 = 0.570 CIDEr pros CIDEr cons Consensus-based — rewards captions matching multiple references Computationally complex at scale (TF-IDF over large sets) TF-IDF weights rare/important words appropriately Sensitive to reference

The interview-grade decision is two-layered: pick autoregressive token generation over diffusion for latency, then split the system into an independently trained tokenizer + generator pair served as separate, separately scalable services (ch8 §Choosing a suitable ML approach, §Overall ML System Design). Requirements & Model Selection ​ Requirements (ch8 §Clarifying Requirements): 5M high-res images of natural scenes/landscapes; unconditional generation (architecture stays prompt-ready); output 1024×1024 or 2048×2048 per request; ~5 s per image — reasonable latency, not real-time. Approach High-res behavior Verdict for 1024²+ @ 5 s VAE / GAN Posterior collapse at ≥512px: the higher-capacity decoder models output independently and ignores the latent space → latents contribute little, diversity drops (ch8 §Choosing a suitable ML approach) Reject Autoregressive Pixel-by-pixel is O(N²) for N×N and hard to parallelize; generating chunk tokens (64×64 px per token → 256 tokens for 1024²) cuts the step count and runs in seconds (ch8 §Choosing a suitable ML approach) Chosen ; diffusion deferred to ch9 Diffusion O(T·N²): super-linear in pixel count, more denoising steps T needed at higher res; standard diffusion takes minutes (ch8 §Choosing a suitable ML approach; footnote 1 — latent diffusion speeds this up, ch10–11) Reject for this latency Image Tokenizer (VQ-VAE) ​ VQ-VAE ( paper ) is a VAE variant purpose-built for tokenization: encode an image into discrete tokens, decode tokens back to an image (ch8 §Image tokenizer). Three parts: Encoder : deep CNN (Conv2D + ReLU stacks) mapping the image to a lower-dimensional continuous latent representation (ch8 §Encoder). Quantizer : an embedding table whose sole parameter is a learnable codebook of k embeddings; each continuous vector is replaced by the nearest codebook entry (Euclidean distance), producing integer token IDs (ch8 §Quantizer). Discretization earns its place twice: (1) avoids posterior collapse — discrete latents force the decoder to use them; (2) shrinks the learning space — the generator predicts among k tokens instead of endless, nearly-identical continuous vectors (ch8 §Avoiding posterior collapse, §Reducing the learning space). Decoder : transposed convolutions ( ConvTranspose2d ) upscale token embeddings back to image size (ch8 §Decoder). Image Generator (Decoder-Only Transformer) ​ Dimension Image tokenizer Image generator Role image ↔ discrete tokens token sequence → next token Training stage I — reconstruction losses II — next-token + cross-entropy Deployed at inference decoder only full model Data it consumes raw images cached token sequences from Stage I Component pipeline: codebook embedding lookup → projection to model dimension → positional encoding (spatial information) → N× blocks (multi-head attention, normalization, feed-forward) → prediction head emitting next-token probabilities (ch8 §Image generator, Fig. 11). Decoder-only chosen because (1) the architecture flexes across modalities — text→text chat, image→text captioning, and image-token generation; (2) attention captures long-range dependencies , which is what keeps generated images coherent (ch8 §Image generator, Fig. 5). Training, Sampling & Serving ​ Stage I losses (ch8 §Stage I: Training the image tokenizer): overall loss is the weighted sum λrec·rec + λquant·quant + λperc·perc + λadv·adv , weights tuned per performance goals (ch8 §Overall loss). Loss Form Why Reconstruction MSE over pixels (ch8 §Reconstruction loss) Pixel fidelity; sufficient at low res Quantization distance between encoder output E(x) and nearest codebook vector; stop-gradient blocks flow through the term so the codebook isn't updated while optimizing the encoder (ch8 §Quantization loss) Pulls encoder outputs toward codebook entries Perceptual distance between pretrained-VGG layer-l feature maps of original vs reconstruction (ch8 §Perceptual loss) High-res images still show artifacts with MSE alone; preserves content/style features Adversarial −log D(x̂) with a discriminator; patch-based variant per VQGAN ( paper ) reduces unnatural artifacts (ch8 §Adversarial loss) Realism Straight-through gradient : the nearest-neighbor lookup has no well-defined gradient; VQ- VAE copies the decoder-input gradient directly to the encoder output, so only selected tokens receive gradients from the decoder (ch8 §Stage I). Image cleaning & normalization (ch8 §Data preparation, step 1 of 2): remove low-quality images — low resolution, excessive noise, irrelevant content — while keeping a wide range of styles, subjects, and compositions; normalize pixel values to 0–1 to stabilize training; resize all images to a uniform 1024×1024 for consistent inputs. Step 2 (tokenization) below. Tokenizer data : training is self-supervised (no labels), so augment the 5M in-house images with LAION-400M for a richer codebook; after training, tokenize all 5M images and cache the token sequences for Stage II (ch8 §Training data). Stage II : next-token prediction with cross-entropy over the cached token sequences (ch8 §Stage II: Training the image generator). Sampling : randomly pick the first token from the codebook as seed → generator predicts the distribution over the codebook → select next token (e.g., top-p) → append → repeat until all 256 tokens exist (1024² at 64×64 px/token) → tokenizer decoder reshapes tokens into the image (ch8 §Sampling). flowchart TD S[Random seed token from codebook] --> G[Generator predicts codebook distribution] G --> T[Pick next token - top-p sampling] T --> C{All 256 tokens generated?} C -- No --> G C -- Yes --> D[Decoding service - tokenizer decoder only] D --> R{2048 requested?} R -- Yes --> SR[Super-resolution service - 2x upscale] R -- No --> U[Return image] SR --> U 🧭 Scenario · Serve 1024-2048px images in five seconds − 100% + ✎ ↺ ◉ {"t

Clarify Requirements First ​ Requirements the interviewer hands you — map every later decision back to one of them (ch9 §Clarifying Requirements): Requirement Value What it drives downstream Resolution 1024×1024 Forces super-resolution cascade — diffusion can't hit this directly Language English first, adaptable Caption filtering + recaptioning rules Training data ~500M image–caption pairs Dedup, NSFW/aesthetic filtering at scale Prompt length Max 128 words Text encoder choice, caching embeddings Latency ~10 s per image Sampling steps, DDIM, distillation, quantization Scope Landscapes → portraits → abstract art Model must be broad, not domain-tuned Fairness Bias on age/race/gender Filters + checks scoped to those attributes Safety Filters offensive/inappropriate output Two gates: prompt safety + harm detection Diffusion vs Autoregressive — Pick One and Defend It ​ Autoregressive: decoder-only Transformer treats the image as a sequence — text tokens in, visual tokens out, an image tokenizer decodes them. Ships as DALL-E and Muse (ch9 § Autoregressive models ). Diffusion : starts from random noise, iteratively denoises toward the prompt; a text encoder (CLIP or T5) produces the embedding that guides each step. x: Section 26 of 26 Text-to-Video Generation Text-to-video is text-to-image with a time axis: 5 s at 24 FPS = 120 frames, and every design choice (latent compression, temporal layers, super-resolution) exists to keep that multiplier affordable. One system, built end-to-end: requirements → LDM → DiT → evaluation → inference pipeline (ch11 §Introduction, §Model Development). Clarifying Requirements (the interview script) ​ Output spec: 5-second, 720p (1280×720), 24 FPS silent videos; a few minutes of generation latency acceptable initially (ch11 §Clarifying Requirements). Data & compute: ~100M video–caption pairs (some noisy/non-English captions); >6000 H100 GPUs; pretrained text-to-image model available to extend (ch11 §Clarifying Requirements). Scope guards: all genres, English-only prompts, audio deferred, safety safeguards mandatory (ch11 §Clarifying Requirements). Why Latent Diffusion (LDM), Not Pixel Diffusion ​ Cost of naive scaling: a 512×512 image ≈ 1 s on an H100; a 720p frame has ~3.6× more pixels, so a 5 s 720p video in pixel space ≈ 7 minutes (ch11 §Choosing a suitable ML approach). LDM idea: train the diffusion model to denoise compressed latent representations instead of pixels; compression network is a separately trained VAE (visual encoder → latents, visual decoder → pixels) ( Stable Diffusion , ch11 §Compression network). Compression math: factor 8 in both spatial and temporal dims: 1280×720×120 frames (110,592,000 px) → 160×90×15 (216,000 px) = 512× smaller , so training is 512× cheaper (ch11 §LDM, Fig. 6). Generation loop: random latent noise → iteratively denoise conditioned on text-encoder embeddings → visual decoder maps latents back to pixels (ch11 §Sampling, Fig. 22). Data Preparation ​ Video filtering: drop low-resolution/short/slow-motion/compression-artifact clips (Movie Gen practice), deduplicate ( LAION dedup ), remove harmful videos with harm-detection models (ch11 §Filter inappropriate videos). Standardization: split into 5 s clips, re-encode to 24 FPS, resize/crop to 1280×720 (ch11 §Standardize videos). Precompute latents: running frames through the VAE every training step is too slow — cache latents for all videos. Caption prep: generate captions for missing/non-English ones and re-caption existing ones with video captioners (LLaMa3-Video, LLaVA) — Sora showed re-captioning is essential for text alignment; precompute caption embeddings with the text encoder (ch11 §Caption preparation). Architecture: U-Net vs DiT ​ Image U-Net is spatial-only: Conv2D + cross-attention blocks model within-frame relations; extending to video means interleaving temporal attention (attend across frames) and temporal convolution (3D conv) into every down/up block (ch11 §U-Net for videos, Fig. 11-13). DiT pipeline: patchify (3D patches for video) → positional encoding → Transformer with cross-attention on text conditioning → unpatchify (LayerNorm → linear → reshape) (ch11 §DiT for videos, Fig. 14-19). Dimension U-Net DiT Backbone Convolutions + temporal attn/conv layers Pure Transformer (patchify/unpatchify) Maturity Longer-tested; Stable Video Diffusion, Emu Video Newer, superior results; Sora, Movie Gen Scaling Around longer, extensively tested — no scaling claim made Scales with data + compute (Transformer property) Modality flexibility Needs temporal modules interleaved Easy — sequences accept any patch type Pick — DiT (follows Sora) (ch11 §U-Net vs. DiT ) Positional encoding: no single best scheme — 1D vs 3D coordinates must be validated empirically; follow OpenSora's RoPE choice ( RoPE , ch11 §Positional encoding). Training ​ One iteration: sample timestep → add noise to latents → DiT predicts the noise (conditioned on text + timestep) → MSE reconstruction loss against the actual noise (ch11 §Training). Video–text data scarcity: two remedies — (1) treat every image as a single-frame video and train jointly on image+video data, or (2) pretrain on image–text, finetune on video–text. Pick (1): one training stage (ch11 §Lack of large-scale video–text training data, Fig. 20). t: What replaces coding puzzles in the internal A3 assessment?

t: Name the 5-part structure for presenting your project.

Your manager (sponsorship) plus a readiness review.

t: What is the single biggest defense mistake?

t: What do window functions do that GROUP BY cannot?
x: Keep every row while computing a value over a related frame — no collapse.

t: Name the canonical dedup pattern for latest record per key.

t: Why are aggregates illegal in WHERE?

x: Fans out rows and silently doubles the total.

t: Name two causes of driver OOM.
x: `collect()` and `toPandas()` pulling full results into driver RAM (also oversized `take()`).

t: Name three causes of executor OOM.
x: One giant partition (skew), `repartition(1)` before a heavy stage, cache without MEMORY_AND_DISK.

t: State the quorum rule and what it guarantees.
x: R + W > N forces read/write overlap so reads see the newest write; W > N/2 prevents split-brain.

t: Availability of W=3/R=3 vs W=1/R=5 on N=5?

t: Why do windows close on event time + watermarks?

t: Why is 2PC a poor fit across services?
x: It blocks — a crashed coordinator leaves locks held; use sagas with compensating transactions.

t: What does the ingestion layer do?
x: Only transport — no business logic; the choices are pull vs push and full vs incremental.

t: Why is log-based CDC the OLTP default?
x: Captures hard deletes at minimal source overhead with seconds latency; polling misses deletes, triggers slow every write.

x: W is the min across partitions, so a stalled source stalls watermark progress everywhere.

x: Side output or dead-letter queue; within lateness, re-accumulate and re-fire as a retraction.

t: Name the four Stage I tokenizer losses.
x: Reconstruction, quantization, perceptual, adversarial — pixel fidelity, codebook commitment, features, realism.

t: How do gradients flow through the quantizer?
x: Straight-through — nearest-neighbor has no gradient, so decoder gradients copy to the encoder.
64×64 px per token → 256 sequential generation steps.

t: Why split generation and decoding services?
x: Distinct computational profiles and latencies — each scales independently.
Generate at 1024², then a pretrained 2× super-resolution upscaler (RCAN/ESRGAN).

t: Why diffusion over autoregressive for text-to-image?
x: Superior fine detail plus a tunable sampling-steps dial — complexity traded for quality.

t: What does the model predict during training?
x: The noise ε, not the clean image x₀ — predicting x₀ underperforms.

t: How does the prompt steer denoising?
x: Cross-attention — queries from image features, keys/values from text-encoder embeddings.
Classifier-free guidance for prompt adherence; DDIM cuts steps from 1,000 to ~20.
Diffusion can't generate high resolution directly — train low, upscale 64→256→1024.
Prompt filtering before compute misses model-generated harm — output harm detection catches it after generation.

t: Which online metric reveals hidden dissatisfaction?
x: Average cost per user per month — unhappy users re-roll seeds, compounding compute spend.
Identity preservation is the product — 10–20 images give richer identity than one reference image.

t: Rank the three methods by identity fidelity.
x: DreamBooth (full finetune) > LoRA (low-rank delta) > textual inversion (one token embedding).
15-min finetune fits the <1h async SLA and models are discarded after the 50 headshots.

t: Why a rare token instead of a common word?
x: Common words carry meanings the model must overwrite; rare tokens are distinct yet tokenizer-cohesive.
Reconstruction on "[V] person" plus class-specific prior preservation on "a person".

t: Why add generic face images to training?
x: Prevents overfitting to one identity and forgetting the generic face class.

t: Why isn't CLIP enough for identity?
x: CLIP/DINO score semantics and detail, not identity — a face recognition model closes the gap.
VAE compresses 8× spatial and 8× temporal — 512× smaller, making training and inference affordable.
~7 minutes per video on an H100 — 120 frames at 3.6× image pixels.
Per-step VAE encoding stalls training — ~200 TB cache for 100M videos buys it back.

t: Why DiT over U-Net for video?
x: 3D patchify with Transformer scaling and modality flexibility — Sora and Movie Gen chose it.

t: How do you handle scarce video–text pairs?
x: Fold images in as single-frame videos — one joint training stage.
FVD — Fréchet distance over I3D features; FID/IS score frames and miss motion.
Spatial SR restores 720p; temporal SR interpolates 12 FPS to 24 FPS.
